alignment.note: Greek pairs the imperfect ἔλεγεν with both the connective Καὶ and the postpositive δέ (a redundant double connective, idiomatic in Markan and Lukan Greek); the Vulgate reduces this to Et dicebat, and the Peshitta to a single ܘ- prefix on ܘܐܡܪ, neither rendering the doubled particle.

Greek prefixes the personal name with the nominative article (ὁ Ἰησοῦς), a Greek convention for proper nouns; Syriac ܝܫܘܥ and Latin Jesus carry no article, since neither language requires one before names.

The Clementine Vulgate inserts a colon after Jesus to mark the onset of direct speech; the Greek ὅτι (recitativum) performs the equivalent function lexically, while Syriac marks the boundary with no overt token.

Greek ὅτι here is recitative, introducing the quoted saying; the Vulgate renders it literally as Quia, retaining the conjunction before direct discourse. The Peshitta omits any corresponding particle, beginning the saying directly with ܠܝܬ.
Greek οὐκ ἔστιν and Latin non est express the negated copula analytically; Syriac ܠܝܬ is the lexicalised negative existential particle, fusing negation and 'to be' into one word.

Greek uses the single privative adjective ἄτιμος ('without honour'); the Vulgate analyses it into a prepositional phrase sine honore, and the Peshitta employs the relative-marked adjective ܕܨܥܝܪ ('who is despised/lowly'), shifting the nuance toward contempt rather than mere lack of honour.
Greek εἰ μή and Syriac ܐܠܐ ܐܢ are two-word exceptive constructions; the Vulgate condenses both into the single conjunction nisi, all conveying 'except'.

Greek ἐν τῇ πατρίδι αὐτοῦ and Latin in patria sua denote the prophet's native country/homeland; the Peshitta ܒܡܕܝܢܬܗ (root d-y-n, 'his city/town') narrows the referent to a single urban locality rather than the broader fatherland, a recurrent Syriac lexical choice for πατρίς.

Greek orders the three domains as hometown, kinsfolk, household; the Peshitta places kinsfolk (ܘܒܝܬ ܐܚܝܢܘܗܝ) before household, matching the Greek sequence, whereas the Vulgate transposes the final two clauses to read domo... cognatione, placing house before kindred — a word-order divergence unique to the Latin.

Greek expresses 'in his house' fully with conjunction, preposition, article, noun, and pronoun (καὶ ἐν τῇ οἰκίᾳ αὐτοῦ); the Peshitta compresses the entire clause into the single inflected word ܘܒܒܝܬܗ (waw + preposition + 'house' + 3ms suffix), and the Vulgate uses et in domo sua, both economising on the Greek's analytic structure.
